source.title: The economics of accuracy for medical reasoning with large language models

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares medical question-answering accuracy across model sizes, which bears on downstream performance versus scale, but it does not measure held-out pretraining loss or reproduce the original scaling-law method.
record.gate_note: The study reports medical QA accuracy across model sizes and prompting conditions, not held-out cross-entropy, training tokens, training compute, or a compute-optimal allocation. Its fitted accuracy framework is explicitly described as in-sample and not validated on held-out models or datasets. Rows below record selected size comparisons for direct answering and PCCR-1024 across the reported datasets/context conditions. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: In medical multiple-choice QA, the study reports how accuracy changes across three sizes of one family (Gemma-3 1B/4B/27B; MedGemma 4B/27B) in several dataset, context and prompt conditions. It also fits accuracy as log-linear in parameters. This bears on V6 in a new domain setting. It does not measure pretraining loss, compute or allocation, so V1–V5 and V7 are untouched. It is not T2 because it does not aim at the original question with a different scaling method; it is a size comparison in a downstream application.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that scale matters but is partly fungible with retrieval context, medical fine-tuning and test-time reasoning. Small models with oracle context can match fine-tuned 27B models. Without context, larger fine-tuned models with extended reasoning remain necessary for the highest accuracy. Their accuracy equations are in-sample descriptions specific to Gemma/MedGemma and these datasets, not validated predictive models. No configuration passes the medical exam.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates benchmark accuracy across model sizes and inference configurations, rather than fitting held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling laws or optimizing parameter/token allocation under a compute budget.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed size-accuracy pattern varies with dataset, context availability, and prompting strategy. The paper also notes that findings may be architecture-specific and reports no temperature sensitivity sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: Accuracy rises with an enforced inference-time reasoning budget without context. A saturating exponential fits it in-sample (pooled R2=0.92). With oracle context it peaks at 128–256 tokens and then declines by 7–13 pp. Test-time compute lets 1B match 4B, but not 4B match 27B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream accuracy scales predictably with test-time compute (reasoning tokens), partly substituting for parameters.

record.problems: The measured outcome is multiple-choice accuracy rather than pretraining loss. Only one model family and three QA datasets were studied; the authors state that their fitted framework is not predictive validation and lacks cross-family or held-out validation. PubMedQA context is oracle context, and several size comparisons are flat or non-monotonic.
record.rows_left_out: The full tables include P1, P2, and intermediate PCCR budgets for all listed models and datasets (Tables 2, 4, and 7), as well as further comparisons of fine-tuning and context. These were not extracted because of the 60-row limit; the selected P0 and PCCR-1024 rows retain direct-answer baselines, extended-reasoning endpoints, dataset/context differences, and size-trend reversals.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss is measured; no power law in parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs. The log-accuracy fit is explicitly in-sample (3 points, 2 parameters).
No variation of shape at fixed parameter count.
No loss scaling in other modalities or regimes. MedGemma fine-tuning is compared only for its accuracy gain, not as a scaling law.

Does not relate accuracy to pretraining loss and does not test out-of-sample prediction. Only three sizes of one family. Size is confounded with training-data differences between Gemma-3 variants (1B text-only).
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: Log-linear fit of baseline accuracy vs size: A = 14.4·log10(S) + 21.6 on MIRAGE P0 for the three Gemma-3 sizes. MAE ≈ 0.5 pp, pooled R2 = 0.95; authors call it an in-sample consistency check, not extrapolation.
Size comparisons under P1, P2 and intermediate PCCR budgets. These are declared in rows_left_out but include further size reversals, e.g. Gemma-3 1B P2 63.1 vs Gemma-3 27B P0 60.0 with context.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3, since this is a downstream application setting rather than an alternative scaling-law method. Size is confounded with other differences: the Gemma-3 variants differ in training data and multimodality (1B is text-only), and only three sizes are tested, so none of this bears on a loss scaling law. Several PubMedQA size reversals for base Gemma-3 may reflect answer-format or prior effects on this yes/no/maybe task rather than capability. Accuracy is scored by an LLM judge (Mistral Small 3.1), validated at κ=0.99 on 200 items. The record's limits_scope group r16–r25 mixed MedGemma gains (r20) with flat Gemma-3 rows, so it has been regrouped.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law fit and range.
Prediction of much larger-run loss from fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation as compute changes.
Architecture depth, width, or other design changes at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning effects on loss, or transfer.

The study measures downstream QA accuracy across sizes, but does not fit or validate a predictive scaling relationship, compare accuracy with pretraining loss, or test transfer to other downstream task families.
It does not test scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation under alternative parameter-counting, training-schedule, data, or fitting choices.

relationships.condition: MIRAGE (no context) and the Israeli medical licensing exam (no context), Gemma-3 and MedGemma series, P0 and PCCR-1024
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises with size, mostly well beyond the CIs: r02, r03, r05, r08, r10, r32, r33, r35, r37, r40. The exceptions are r07 (small) and r38 (flat).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy generally rises beyond the confidence intervals, with exceptions showing small or flat gains.

relationships.condition: PubMedQA, MedGemma 4B→27B, no context (P0, PCCR-1024) and oracle context PCCR-1024
relationships.reason: MedGemma 27B beats 4B by about 6–11 pp in these conditions (r15, r20, r30).
relationships.display_finding: On PubMedQA, MedGemma 27B outperforms 4B by about 6–11 percentage points in the tested context and prompting conditions.

relationships.condition: PubMedQA, Gemma-3 base series, all four context/prompt conditions
relationships.reason: Accuracy falls with size in two conditions: P0 without context (40.2→24.2→21.2, r11–r13) and 4B→27B with oracle context under PCCR-1024 (r28). It is flat within CI in the other two (r16–r18, r21–r23).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy fell with size under P0 without context (40.2→24.2→21.2) and from 4B to 27B with oracle context under PCCR-1024; differences remained within confidence intervals in the other two conditions.

relationships.condition: PubMedQA with oracle context, MedGemma 4B→27B, P0
relationships.reason: No size gain beyond CI: 73.1→74.7 (r24, r25).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased from 73.1 to 74.7, a difference within confidence intervals.

relationships.condition: Gemma-3 4B→27B and 1B→4B on MIRAGE and the exam under PCCR-1024 versus P0
relationships.reason: The size gain depends on prompting. Under P0, 1B→4B on MIRAGE gains 9.5 pp (r02) but only 2.9 pp under PCCR-1024 (r07). Under P0, Gemma-3 4B→27B on the exam gains 12.4 pp (r33) but under PCCR-1024 the change (r38) is within CI.
relationships.display_finding: MIRAGE gains from 1B to 4B shrank from 9.5 percentage points under P0 to 2.9 under PCCR-1024, while the 4B→27B exam gain shrank from 12.4 points to within the confidence interval.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
